newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: U.N.'s Annan to visit Mandela on Timor initiative.
newsitem.headline: U.N.'s Annan to visit Mandela on Timor initiative.

text.p: U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan will visit President Nelson Mandela on Friday to discuss their joint initiative to end the conflict in Indonesian-ruled East Timor, officials said on Monday.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Pieter Swanepoel said South Africa was told on Monday that Annan and not a U.N. envoy would arrive for the midday meeting in Pretoria.
Government sources said Annan's surprise decision probably signalled an acceleration of the U.N.'s bid to end the conflict in East Timor.

Earlier on Monday, two government sources confirmed separately to Reuters that South Africa had expelled Portuguese Ambassador Vasco Valente last week in response to Indonesian protests about a letter that went astray.

The sources said Lisbon had been given 48 hours to withdraw Valente after it was confirmed he had received and failed to forward or return a letter from Mandela to Indonesian President Suharto, which was delivered to his embassy by mistake.
"There has been a slight mistake on the part of one individual and he has been asked to leave," said one source, adding that diplomatic relations with Portugal remained intact.

In the letter, Mandela asked Suharto to release jailed rebel leader Xanana Gusmao as a first step towards ending the conflict in East Timor, a former Portuguese colony over which Indonesia has assumed control.
Details of the letter were published in Portuguese newspapers before Suharto knew of its existence, undermining Mandela's effort to assist the U.N.'s peace initiative.
Joel Netshitenzhe, Mandela's senior spokesman, declined to confirm or deny that Valente had been expelled, but added:
"The matter has now been resolved and the letter has been received by the Indonesian president and government. The process that President Mandela initiated is proceeding smoothly."

East Timor is the third international conflict in which Mandela has sought personally to intervene. He has tried also to help bring democracy to Nigeria and he sought to mediate a peaceful transfer of power in the former Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Mandela visited Suharto last month and won permission to meet jailed rebel leader Xanana Gusmao. After his return, he wrote to Suharto asking for the rebel leader's release and inviting the Indonesian President to South Africa in November.
He also invited East Timorese bishop and Nobel peace laureate Ximenes Belo to visit him in South Africa.
Valente was the first foreign diplomat expelled since 1994, when Mandela won the country's first democratic elections.

Presidential spokesman Parks Mankahlana said South Africa would not comment on any aspect of the incident over the misdirected letter, adding that it had since been received by Suharto and that the peace process was on track.
"It is something that has to be dealt with very cautiously. President Suharto and all the other parties must dictate the terms of forward movement, not President Mandela," he said.
"The President really sees this as a medium to long-term effort. It is not something that can be resolved quickly."
